events_chronological: As a young conscript a soldier lands on the coast with an armoured column.
His unit fires all night at a car approaching a roadblock and finds a family inside it at first light.
A comrade swims out to sea from a burning landing craft and lives when the rest of his unit does not.
Another soldier dances with a machine gun down a boulevard under sniper fire, beneath posters of an assassinated leader.
The unit shells an orchard and a boy carrying a rocket launcher is killed in front of them.
The soldier and two others bathe in the sea at night under flares while the city burns behind them.
Armed irregulars go into the refugee camps while the soldiers outside send up flares to light the sky for them.
Over two days the militia kill the people in the camps, while the soldiers on the roofs fail to grasp what they are watching.
The soldier stands at the edge of the camp as the women come out screaming.
More than twenty years on, a friend tells him over a drink about a recurring dream of twenty-six dogs.
He realises he remembers nothing whatever of the war and sets out to find the men he served with.
A psychologist explains to him that memory can be assembled out of what a person needs rather than what occurred.
A television reporter tells him what he saw in the camps and what he said to the defence minister on the telephone.
He understands that the flare-lit memory of himself in the sea is a screen he built to stand between himself and the camps.
nonlinear_category_reason: No timeline dominates, the scenes do not fall into two alternating bands, and no non-temporal principle groups them into blocks; the order is associative, so none of the other six shapes applies. A man with no memory of a war reassembles it out of other men's accounts, so the fragments arrive in the order they are recovered rather than the order they happened.
syuzhet_notes: The telling moves between present-day interviews, the war as each man recalls it, and dreams that turn out to be inventions, with nothing distinguishing them. Some scenes are established as false memories only after being shown as fact.
fabula_notes: The war chronology is fixed by the campaign's own sequence. The interviews are undated relative to one another, and the sea scene is placed where the work finally establishes it belongs.

events.content: As a young conscript he enters the coastal campaign inside a machine whose direction and consequences he does not yet understand.
